commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether contract terms requiring vendor monitoring, timed notification of incidents and model changes, and shared monitoring evidence reduce hidden degradation of deployed AI. The recommendation rests on 12 listed endorsements, made up of one framework rated must and 11 guidance or commentary sources rated should.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice and none documents the hazard, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence. Of the 12 listed endorsements, 8 are commentaries, 3 are guidance documents, and 1 is a framework, and only the CHAI framework uses must language. Agreement across these sources reflects expert opinion, which GRADE does not treat as evidence of effect.

The supplied record contains no measurement of how often vendor-side changes or degradation go undetected by deploying sites, or of any harm that followed. Without such data, the size of the failure mode and the share of problems a notification clause might catch before they reach patients remain unknown.

The endorsements differ in scope. The CHAI language addresses misuse and unauthorized disclosure, while one commentary calls for mandatory notification of model updates and defined revalidation triggers. None of the listed sources specifies notification timeframes or the form that shared monitoring evidence should take, so health systems drafting contracts would need to set these terms themselves.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare sites with and without contractual monitoring and notification terms, measuring time from a vendor model change or degradation to site awareness, the frequency of unplanned performance checks, and downstream patient outcomes. Descriptive work on how often vendor changes currently go unreported would also establish the size of the hazard.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence exists on its effect in Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One commentary on rural Australian hospitals calls for vendor monitoring tools suited to rural services, which suggests that smaller or under-resourced systems may face different contracting conditions, though this remains untested.
